值得閱讀的理由

  • 從魯賓花瓶與雙眼競爭出發，清楚說明研究者如何區分外界刺激與主觀知覺。
  • 整理全球神經工作空間理論與整合資訊理論的爭論，以及雙方共同設計的大型對抗性實驗結果。
  • 介紹曹多麗絲團隊如何以「無報告範式」排除決策與動作等干擾，並提出意識可能具有快速時間變化的觀點。

摘要

意識究竟藏在哪裡？

作者以經典的魯賓花瓶錯覺開場：同一幅圖像可能被看成花瓶，也可能被看成彼此相對的兩張臉；圖像沒有改變，改變的是觀看者的知覺。神經科學家因此追問，哪些神經活動與我們實際意識到的內容相對應，這個問題稱為意識的神經相關物。自法蘭西斯・克里克在晚年推動意識研究以來，雙眼競爭一直是常用工具：左右眼看到不同圖像，知覺便在兩者間交替，即使外界刺激維持不變。

兩派理論與對抗性實驗

對意識訊號位於何處，研究者主要分成兩派。全球神經工作空間理論認為，感官資訊必須在前額葉等區域引發「點燃」並廣播至全腦，才會進入意識；整合資訊理論則主張，後部感官皮質本身的高度整合結構就足以支持意識。由於不同實驗方法容易偏向不同理論，雙方曾共同預先登錄預測與判敗條件，合作進行大規模對抗性實驗。

這項研究讓256名受試者觀看不同時長的視覺刺激，並以功能性磁振造影、腦磁圖及顱內腦電圖記錄反應。結果並未明確支持任何一方：後部皮質沒有呈現整合資訊理論預測的持續同步活動；前額葉也未在刺激消失時出現預期的「點燃」訊號，對部分意識內容的解碼能力亦有限。於是，意識究竟位於大腦哪個區域，仍陷於僵局。

從腦區轉向時間

作者接著介紹曹多麗絲團隊的一項研究：團隊在猴子實驗中發現，即使影像與猴子的主觀知覺看似維持不變，同一群神經元仍會以每秒約15次的頻率，在意識與無意識表徵之間切換。這項發現提出另一種可能：意識訊號未必藏在某個特定腦區，而可能存在於神經活動的短暫時間片段中。論文第一作者Janis Hesse也形容，意識或許更取決於神經活動「何時」發生，而非「在哪裡」發生。

曹多麗絲以研究猴腦中的臉孔區塊系統聞名。她與合作者發現，猴子的下顳葉有多個專門處理臉孔的區域，分工處理視角等特徵；團隊也進一步解析臉孔的神經編碼方式，並曾利用約200個神經元的活動重建猴子所見的臉孔。作者指出，這種解讀神經元訊息的能力，為團隊轉向研究意識奠定了基礎。

無須回報的意識測量

過去的雙眼競爭實驗常要求猴子按下拉桿，報告自己看見哪個影像，但這會混入決策、動作規劃等活動，使研究者難以判定測得的訊號究竟來自知覺本身，還是「報告知覺」的過程。瞳孔變化與眼球反射等替代指標也各有侷限。曹多麗絲與Hesse因此設計無報告範式：猴子只需追隨跳動的注視點，研究者再以眼球運動推斷牠正在注意哪個影像，不必訓練牠執行知覺回報任務。

研究顯示，這種方法在人類受試者中的推斷準確率平均達93%；兩隻未受過回報訓練的猴子，也只花一兩天便學會任務。研究者發現，下顳葉臉孔區塊中的部分神經元會追蹤意識知覺的變化：ML區約57%的細胞、AM區約73%的細胞與知覺覺察有關，支持這些區域存在真正的意識神經相關物。然而，團隊仍能解碼猴子意識到與未意識到的影像，代表純粹只屬於意識本身的訊號依舊難以分離。

仍未解開的矛盾

作者指出，這項發現延續了一個困擾研究者多年的矛盾：教科書常認為前額葉負責形成純粹的意識表徵，但雙眼競爭研究在不同腦區測得的活動，與意識之間往往只有有限關聯。早期研究曾指出，下顳葉大多數神經元會隨知覺變化，但相關反應在雙眼競爭時，弱於兩張圖像分別呈現、交替切換時的反應。這究竟代表猴子回報不準確，還是單一神經元同時混合多種訊息？影片字幕在此處中斷，尚未提供後續解釋。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. First, imagine an image: a white vase, or perhaps two black profiles facing each other. This is the classic Rubin vase optical illusion. Stare at it, and you'll see the image flicker back and forth between a vase and faces. The key is that the image itself never changes; what changes is your perception. So the question is, where in the brain, and how, is this choice made for us? Which specific neural activity corresponds to what we actually perceive? In neuroscience,. this question has a specific name: the Neural Correlates of Consciousness. In the 1990s, Francis Crick, Nobel laureate and co-discoverer of the DNA double helix, turned his attention to consciousness in his later years, pushing the field to search for neural activity that directly corresponds to conscious experience. For over 30 years , a common tool used by researchers is "binocular rivalry." By showing your left and right eyes two different images—for example, a face on one side and an object on the other—you won't see them overlaid, but will instead see them alternating. The physical input remains constant, yet. conscious perception changes. This allows us to isolate consciousness signals from pure sensory processing signals. So where exactly is this signal hidden in the brain? The field is split into two camps. One is the " Global Neuronal Workspace Theory," which posits that consciousness depends on a broadcast network centered in the prefrontal cortex; sensory information only enters consciousness once it is ignited and broadcast to the whole brain for various systems to use. Information not broadcasted remains forever in the unconscious background. The other camp, Integrated Information Theory, argues that the sensory cortex in the back of the brain is sufficient. on its own, meaning the highly integrated connection structure of the posterior cortex is independent of prefrontal broadcasting. Each side has its own evidence, and after years of debate, neither has been able to convince the other. There is also an unspoken issue in academia: whether a theory finds supporting evidence often depends heavily on the experimental methods used. Everyone tends to design experiments that favor their own theory , making confirmation bias inevitable. Recently, the two camps did something quite rare in the scientific community: they sat down and jointly designed a large-scale adversarial experiment. Led by a neutral coalition, the theorists.

and experimental teams pre-registered everything: where their predictions differed, and which results would constitute a failure for each side, so that no one could move the goalposts later. The conclusions of this 2025 showdown were published in Nature. 256 subjects participated in the experiment , utilizing fMRI, MEG, and intracranial EEG to record their neural responses while they viewed visual stimuli of varying durations. The results, however , were somewhat awkward. The posterior cortex failed to show the sustained synchronous activity predicted by Integrated Information Theory, which challenged the claim that network. connectivity determines consciousness. Meanwhile, in the frontal regions, the theoretically expected "ignition" signal did not appear when the stimuli vanished, and the representation of certain dimensions of consciousness was limited, managing to decode only parts of the conscious content. The result was that the core predictions of both sides lacked sufficient support, leaving consciousness research deadlocked on the question of location. Then, on October 16, 2026, neuroscientist Doris Tsao's team at UC Berkeley published a paper on bioRxiv that answered this question from a different dimension—not space, but time. In their macaque experiments, they discovered that even when the. image remained constant and the monkey's subjective perception remained unchanged, the same group of neurons in the brain would switch back and forth between conscious and unconscious representations about 15 times per second. In other words, the pure consciousness signal that researchers had been desperately seeking for years was not hidden in a specific brain region, but rather within the timeline —hidden in transient temporal fragments. Tsao herself subsequently posted over a dozen threads on X to introduce this work. The very first sentence stated that this was a completely unexpected discovery, one that upends our understanding of the biological basis of consciousness built over decades and brings us a significant step closer to the recipe. for generating conscious experience. The paper's lead author, Janis Hesse, also posted that this was the most important discovery of his career: your brain switches between conscious and unconscious modes about 15 times per second. Consciousness may not depend on where neural activity occurs in the brain, but rather on when it occurs. Speaking of Doris Tsao, those who follow brain science should not be unfamiliar with her. She studied biology and math as an undergraduate at Caltech and received her Ph.D. in neuroscience from Harvard in 2002. Her most famous work is the discovery of the "face patch" system in the macaque brain. In the macaque's inferotemporal cortex, there are multiple small.

regions specialized for processing faces, connected and organized by division of labor; the earlier patches are sensitive to the viewing angle, while the later ones become increasingly invariant to perspective. Even more impressively, she and her collaborators cracked the neural code of faces: a face is represented in neurons as a single point within a multi-dimensional feature space. Some cells are dedicated to the distance between eyes, while others are specifically for hair presence. In 2017 , his team analyzed only about 200 neurons 'firing patterns to reconstruct the face the monkey was viewing with remarkable accuracy. In 2024, he was awarded the Kavli Prize in Neuroscience. alongside Nancy Kanwisher from MIT and Winrich Freiwald from Rockefeller University. The citation recognized their discovery of a highly localized and specialized face-representation system in the primate cerebral cortex. Kanwisher was the one who used brain imaging to locate the human fusiform face area in 1997; Freiwald and Tsao were inspired to find the corresponding patch system in macaque brains. It can be said that this very ability to " understand what neurons are saying" paved the way for today's consciousness research. In recent years, Tsao has gradually shifted his focus toward the problem of consciousness. Currently, he serves as the Lead Scientist for the. neuroscience program at the non-profit research institution, the Astera Institute, aiming to decipher the specific mechanisms by which the brain generates conscious experience, cognition, and intelligent behavior. The seeds for this discovery were actually sown back in 2020, when Tsao collaborated with Hesse, then a PhD student at Caltech, to publish a study in*Nature*. Past binocular rivalry experiments required training monkeys to press levers to report which image they were currently seeing. But this introduced a confounding factor: was the neural activity you measured reflecting the act of seeing itself, or merely the action of reporting? One must realize that reporting involves a. whole range of processes, such as decision-making and motor planning. Researchers have used brain imaging to compare and found that once subjects are not required to report actively, the activity in many high-level brain regions linked to perception disappears , leading one to question how much of the previously measured "consciousness signals" were just reporting signals. Previously, others had tried non-report methods, such as utilizing how pupil size changes with the brightness of the dominant image, or how the eyes reflexively track the motion direction of the dominant stimulus; however, pupils are also affected by arousal and surprise, and that kind of ocular.

reflex persists even in anesthetized monkeys, making it hard to claim it has much to do with consciousness. Tsao and Hesse devised a much cleaner method, called the no-report paradigm. They placed a fixation point that jumps between locations in both images; the monkey simply needs to follow the fixation point in the eye that it is currently seeing. Children instinctively look at whichever image catches their eye. Without teaching them any reporting tasks, we can infer which image they are conscious of simply by tracking their eye movements. This method has now been verified in human subjects, with an average. inference accuracy of 93%. The two experimental monkeys had never been trained to report their perception, yet they learned this simple task in just a day or two. They found that neurons in the inferior temporal face patches track changes in conscious perception, with 57%of cells in the ML patch and 73 %in the AM patch encoding awareness— no reporting required. This confirms that genuine neural correlates of consciousness exist in the inferior temporal cortex. However, in the same experiment, they could decode both the image the monkey was conscious of and the one it wasn't; that pure signal. belonging solely to consciousness remained elusive. This leaves a paradox that has troubled researchers for nearly a decade. The classic textbook view suggests a region in the frontal brain holds pure conscious representations, yet the signals they recorded show a weak correlation with consciousness across all brain areas. Since the 1990s, every experiment recording neurons during binocular rivalry has repeatedly encountered the same phenomenon. A classic 1997 study claimed that 90%of inferior temporal neurons track conscious perception. However, few noticed a detail: the response modulation of these neurons. during rivalry is smaller than when the two images are presented separately and toggled. Does this reduction mean the monkey reported incorrectly, or do single cells mix both representations? The old method of averaging over multiple trials cannot distinguish these two possibilities. The researchers later lamented that they were trapped by their own expectations. So, how did this new study break the deadlock? The method uses a classic paradigm called binocular flash suppression: first, show one image to one eye, then suddenly present a second image to the other eye. The newly appearing image almost always instantly.

captures consciousness. The original image, while still displayed on the screen, vanishes from your perception. The advantage of this paradigm is that researchers can fully control which image is perceived and which is suppressed, letting two rhesus monkeys view thousands of such stimulus pairs. Simultaneously, they inserted neural probes into two inferior temporal face patches and two prefrontal cortex regions. The prefrontal cortex is responsible for advanced cognitive functions like decision-making and planning, which is exactly the area the prefrontal camp identifies as the seat of consciousness. This type of probe can simultaneously capture the firing of hundreds of neurons, and the entire study recorded thousands of neurons in. total. This allows researchers to track the entire neuronal population within a single experiment with millisecond precision, seeing exactly what they are representing at any given moment. Next, I will explain the core discovery of this study in a bit more detail. Using traditional analytical methods— averaging neural activity over a period of time—the strength of the inferior temporal neurons' discrimination of conscious perception remained only about one-quarter of that seen when images were presented physically alone; it was still that same familiar weak signal. But this time, the team took a different approach, slicing each experiment into 10-millisecond segments and continuously determining whether the current population activity pattern. was closer to the template for face A or face B. The result caught everyone by surprise: during the time when both the image and perception were stable, the neuronal population didn't represent only the face you saw; instead, it switched back and forth between representing the seen face and the unseen face about every 60 milliseconds. The research team labeled these two types of time segments as " conscious micro-states" and " unconscious micro-states." When they recalculated the data by splitting it according to these states, the discrimination strength of the neurons for perception returned almost to the level of images presented alone, while the unconscious micro-states showed the. exact opposite, with population activity clearly representing the face that was not seen. In other words, the weak signal measured by everyone over the past 30 years wasn't weak because the signal itself was faint, but because two strong signals in opposite directions canceled each other out in the time-averaged data. The key finding follows: the research team did not find two distinct groups of cells, one dedicated to consciousness and one to the unconscious. The same face-selective cells synchronously switch their tuning preferences every 60 milliseconds or so, meaning they fire for the features of the first face one moment, and for the features of the second face the next. The same group of.

neurons represents what you are conscious of and what you are not conscious of at different moments in time. In the paper, the authors describe their reaction upon seeing the results: when the researchers showed them the images reconstructed from the two states, the activity from the " conscious" micro-states reconstructed the exact face the monkey saw, while the activity from the "unconscious" micro-states reconstructed the face it did not see; both were remarkably accurate. He said he jumped for joy, as a mystery that had troubled him for nearly a decade finally had an answer: in binocular rivalry tasks, they had found a pure consciousness signal as clear as the sense of awareness itself. To rule out the possibility of it being a statistical artifact, they conducted control tests anyway. After removing the images, the conclusion still held, and it wasn't just the inferior temporal lobe; results recorded from the prefrontal cortex were qualitatively the same. Why is this discovery so important? Because it directly undermines the common premise of the aforementioned debate between the two camps. Whether it's the prefrontal camp or the posterior cortex camp, both sides assumed that the consciousness signal resides stably in a specific brain region, arguing only over which one. Chao's team recorded from both the prefrontal and inferior temporal lobes, finding no stably residing consciousness signal in either. ; neurons constantly switched between the two faces, meaning consciousness doesn't live in a specific brain location, but rather in a specific temporal phase. Most past experiments averaged long-duration activity, and the temporal resolution of human imaging is relatively coarse, making it impossible to detect rapid switches every 60 milliseconds; thus, the signals naturally appeared weak and diffuse. What couldn't be found on the spatial map turned out to be written on the timeline. Of course, new answers bring new questions: since the same group of neurons represents both faces in turns, what decides which one we perceive? Following common intuition,. the perceived face should trigger more intense neuronal firing, but data shows the opposite: during the half-time when it's not perceived, the overall firing is actually slightly stronger. The real difference between the two states lies in how sensitive neurons are to changes in facial features. During conscious segments, neuronal responses are sharper and amplified, while during unconscious segments, the same neurons 'responses are flatter. As for what controls this 60-millisecond switching, it remains unclear. The authors speculate it may stem from internal interactions between neurons in the visual cortex, or perhaps regulation from other regions like the parietal.

lobe. The study also features a set of data that specifically highlights the complexity of consciousness mechanisms. The team recorded two face patches in the inferior temporal lobe simultaneously and found their switching rhythms were like beating to their own drums, with very weak correlation between the two, yet we only ever see one image at any given moment. If each brain region switches on its own, how is this unified perception pieced together? That remains a mystery for now. For Cao himself, what’s most exciting about this entire body of work isn’t the conscious half, but the unconscious half. During the time spent being unconscious, the brain still retains. complete and clear facial information, rich enough to reconstruct that face directly. This resonates well with classic findings in psychology: a fearful face flashes across a screen, the subject notices nothing, yet the amygdala, which processes emotions, has already reacted. Although you aren't conscious of what you’ve seen, it still influences your judgment, attention, and emotions. If the brain always keeps the complete content of these unseen things, it’s no surprise they can quietly influence your behavior. So why would the brain expend the effort to preserve an image you didn't actually see? The researchers speculate that during the time you. don’t see it, the brain may be testing other interpretations of the world in the background without disrupting your current behavior; during the time you do see it, it carries the interpretation the brain has adopted, passing it to the brain regions responsible for verbal reflection and action, allowing the same group of neurons to process different information at different times. This mechanism of temporal multiplexing is actually not rare in the brain. Another study published by Cao’s lab in Nature in 2024 found that the same group of neurons in the temporal lobe processes the face you see in front of you and your memory of a familiar face at different moments. When seeing a strange face, they fire. according to one set of encoding axes; after a long latency period, the encoding axes rotate to switch to the set representing familiarity. Perception and memory also coexist by being staggered in time. Therefore, the alternation between consciousness and unconsciousness is likely just another application of this general brain strategy. Finally, it’s time to pour some cold water where it’s needed. This work is currently in the preprint stage and has not undergone peer review . The data comes from two macaques, so whether the conclusions can be generalized to humans and to a wider range of stimuli and scenarios requires more experiments. The research team has indicated that they will release the raw data and analysis code upon the.

paper's formal publication for other labs to verify. Cao himself also posted a clarification, reminding everyone not to overinterpret the findings—for example, they have not proven that consciousness has a specific frame rate . This widely circulated claim is a misreading of the results. More importantly, the current results show correlation; conscious states and this rapid switching appear together, but to prove a causal relationship between them, one must conduct active interventions, such as artificially... ...disrupting this switching to see if perception changes accordingly. The research project at the Astra Institute includes large-scale manipulation of neural circuits, which is aimed. squarely at the "British problem." Looking back over the past 30 years, consciousness research has been searching for answers on the brain's map; the frontal lobe versus the posterior cortex—the two factions are locked in a stalemate, and after a meticulously designed adversarial experiment, the experiment failed to fully prove itself. This work suggests to us that perhaps the question itself was asked in the wrong direction; the answer may not be written in a specific brain region, but rather on the timeline. Ying says that finding a signal that richly represents something you are not conscious of gives us, for the first time, a concrete way to approach the age-old problem of how neural activity enters consciousness. The next question is: with the same group of neurons switching back and forth between two faces every 60 milliseconds, what exactly determines which one we perceive at any given moment? We welcome everyone to share their thoughts in the comments section.

曹多麗絲以研究猴腦中的臉孔區塊系統聞名。她與合作者發現，猴子的下顳葉有多個專門處理臉孔的區域，分工處理視角等特徵；團隊也進一步解析臉孔的神經編碼方式，並曾利用約200個神經元的活動重建猴子所見的臉孔。作者指出，這種解讀神經元訊息的能力，為團隊轉向研究意識奠定了基礎。

Everyone tends to design experiments that favor their own theory , making confirmation bias inevitable. Recently, the two camps did something quite rare in the scientific community: they sat down and jointly designed a large-scale adversarial experiment. Led by a neutral coalition, the theorists.

One must realize that reporting involves a. whole range of processes, such as decision-making and motor planning. Researchers have used brain imaging to compare and found that once subjects are not required to report actively, the activity in many high-level brain regions linked to perception disappears , leading one to question how much of the previously measured "consciousness signals" were just reporting signals. They placed a fixation point that jumps between locations in both images; the monkey simply needs to follow the fixation point in the eye that it is currently seeing. Children instinctively look at whichever image catches their eye. Without teaching them any reporting tasks, we can infer which image they are conscious of simply by tracking their eye movements. This leaves a paradox that has troubled researchers for nearly a decade. The classic textbook view suggests a region in the frontal brain holds pure conscious representations, yet the signals they recorded show a weak correlation with consciousness across all brain areas. captures consciousness. The original image, while still displayed on the screen, vanishes from your perception. neurons represents what you are conscious of and what you are not conscious of at different moments in time. lobe. The study also features a set of data that specifically highlights the complexity of consciousness mechanisms. Although you aren't conscious of what you’ve seen, it still influences your judgment, attention, and emotions. The researchers speculate that during the time you. don’t see it, the brain may be testing other interpretations of the world in the background without disrupting your current behavior; during the time you do see it, it carries the interpretation the brain has adopted, passing it to the brain regions responsible for verbal reflection and action, allowing the same group of neurons to process different information at different times. paper's formal publication for other labs to verify. This widely circulated claim is a misreading of the results. More importantly, the current results show correlation; conscious states and this rapid switching appear together, but to prove a causal relationship between them, one must conduct active interventions, such as artificially... ...disrupting this switching to see if perception changes accordingly. The research project at the Astra Institute includes large-scale manipulation of neural circuits, which is aimed. squarely at the "British problem." Looking back over the past 30 years, consciousness research has been searching for answers on the brain's map; the frontal lobe versus the posterior cortex—the two factions are locked in a stalemate, and after a meticulously designed adversarial experiment, the experiment failed to fully prove itself. This work suggests to us that perhaps the question itself was asked in the wrong direction; the answer may not be written in a specific brain region, but rather on the timeline. Ying says that finding a signal that richly represents something you are not conscious of gives us, for the first time, a concrete way to approach the age-old problem of how neural activity enters consciousness. The next question is: with the same group of neurons switching back and forth between two faces every 60 milliseconds, what exactly determines which one we perceive at any given moment? We welcome everyone to share their thoughts in the comments section.

過去的雙眼競爭實驗常要求猴子按下拉桿，報告自己看見哪個影像，但這會混入決策、動作規劃等活動，使研究者難以判定測得的訊號究竟來自知覺本身，還是「報告知覺」的過程。瞳孔變化與眼球反射等替代指標也各有侷限。曹多麗絲與Hesse因此設計無報告範式：猴子只需追隨跳動的注視點，研究者再以眼球運動推斷牠正在注意哪個影像，不必訓練牠執行知覺回報任務。

研究顯示，這種方法在人類受試者中的推斷準確率平均達93%；兩隻未受過回報訓練的猴子，也只花一兩天便學會任務。研究者發現，下顳葉臉孔區塊中的部分神經元會追蹤意識知覺的變化：ML區約57%的細胞、AM區約73%的細胞與知覺覺察有關，支持這些區域存在真正的意識神經相關物。然而，團隊仍能解碼猴子意識到與未意識到的影像，代表純粹只屬於意識本身的訊號依舊難以分離。

仍未解開的矛盾

作者指出，這項發現延續了一個困擾研究者多年的矛盾：教科書常認為前額葉負責形成純粹的意識表徵，但雙眼競爭研究在不同腦區測得的活動，與意識之間往往只有有限關聯。早期研究曾指出，下顳葉大多數神經元會隨知覺變化，但相關反應在雙眼競爭時，弱於兩張圖像分別呈現、交替切換時的反應。這究竟代表猴子回報不準確，還是單一神經元同時混合多種訊息？影片字幕在此處中斷，尚未提供後續解釋。

lobe. The study also features a set of data that specifically highlights the complexity of consciousness mechanisms. The researchers speculate that during the time you. don’t see it, the brain may be testing other interpretations of the world in the background without disrupting your current behavior; during the time you do see it, it carries the interpretation the brain has adopted, passing it to the brain regions responsible for verbal reflection and action, allowing the same group of neurons to process different information at different times. Another study published by Cao’s lab in Nature in 2024 found that the same group of neurons in the temporal lobe processes the face you see in front of you and your memory of a familiar face at different moments. When seeing a strange face, they fire. according to one set of encoding axes; after a long latency period, the encoding axes rotate to switch to the set representing familiarity. Finally, it’s time to pour some cold water where it’s needed. This work is currently in the preprint stage and has not undergone peer review . The data comes from two macaques, so whether the conclusions can be generalized to humans and to a wider range of stimuli and scenarios requires more experiments. The research team has indicated that they will release the raw data and analysis code upon the.

paper's formal publication for other labs to verify. This widely circulated claim is a misreading of the results. More importantly, the current results show correlation; conscious states and this rapid switching appear together, but to prove a causal relationship between them, one must conduct active interventions, such as artificially... ...disrupting this switching to see if perception changes accordingly. The research project at the Astra Institute includes large-scale manipulation of neural circuits, which is aimed. squarely at the "British problem." Looking back over the past 30 years, consciousness research has been searching for answers on the brain's map; the frontal lobe versus the posterior cortex—the two factions are locked in a stalemate, and after a meticulously designed adversarial experiment, the experiment failed to fully prove itself. The next question is: with the same group of neurons switching back and forth between two faces every 60 milliseconds, what exactly determines which one we perceive at any given moment? 值得閱讀的理由

  • 探討現代車企如何將汽車開發週期從傳統的 4 到 5 年大幅縮短至 18 到 24 個月。
  • 詳細分析造車過程中的核心環節（如對標車、立項、模具、電池包、冬測及平台化等）與時間成本。
  • 提供關於汽車產業加速競爭的深入觀點與結語反思。

摘要

這部由「最佳拍档」頻道的影片主題為《解密：速成车是怎么造出来的》 [[00:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=1)]，探討了汽車製造業中「速成車」的誕生邏輯與開發過程。影片指出，傳統上開發一款全新車系需要 4 到 5 年（例如 2015 年的標準），而現代某些車型則能壓縮至 18 到 24 個月（例如 2025 年的標準），甚至達到「前 5000 台不賺錢、車型投入幾億元」的規模 [[00:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=5)]。

核心開發階段與對標

影片中展示了對標車的概念，透過參考現有車型來調整定位與價格 [[00:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=14)]，並提及「立項」階段的策略：跳過越級階段、先開工後補文檔 [[00:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=19)]。在前期調研與驗證階段，最快可在 1 年內完成立項到對標車造車 [[00:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=27)]。此外也列出了 V 模型完整開發、改動成本、定點與量產前的小時數等數據 [[00:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=40)]。

模具與電池包開發

影片隨後拆解了車輛的重要零件，包括沖壓模具（如側圍外板）的開發週期與成本優化 [[00:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=57)]，以及電池包的開發（電芯選型、BOM 階段、實測水準與產線提速） [[01:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=73)]。在電池包與電芯的驗證過程中，經歷了數百次的實測與里程驗證 [[01:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=83)]。

冬測、軟體與平台化

在車輛驗證部分，影片提到了冬測階段（漠河、吐魯番、南半球等季節測試）以及大量的軟體補丁與 OTA 升級與召回次數 [[01:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=103)]。最後則探討了平台化的概念：透過一個平台衍生多車型、共用零件與縮短週期，展現出不同開發模式下的累計銷量差異 [[02:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=135)]。

影片最後總結並引用觀點：「把問題留在實驗室，還是任其流向市場——『没人敢冒慢下来的风险，因为我减速，你就赢了。』」 [[02:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tUL8opbBOUs&t=167)]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OjuLyy5ajYA

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解創業者如何在產品已有營收時，仍判斷市場天花板並果斷轉型。
  • 看見人工智慧如何改變既有產業競爭，也為電子郵件與行事曆等日常工作帶來新機會。
  • 從產品策略、企業導入與使用者體驗，理解打造 AI 助理產品的關鍵取捨。

摘要

看似成功的報稅新創，為何選擇轉型

Da Fei 分享了一段由 Ben Horowitz 與 Garry Tan 的對話引出的故事：Horowitz 說一款名為 Tess 的工具改變了他的生活，Tan 才發現這是 J.D. Greys 的新產品。Greys 曾經營企業報稅新創，也曾擔任 Pliant 執行長，Tan 卻完全不知道他已轉換方向。

2024 年，J.D. 與共同創辦人打造企業報稅產品，讓客戶上傳財務報表、合約等資料，再由模型產出可提交的稅表。報稅流程高度依賴文字與結構化資料，十分適合大型模型處理；產品花了一年打造，第一年營收便達一百萬美元，照原本走勢，第二年可能達到兩百五十萬至三百萬美元。

然而，AI 也讓既有報稅業者能運用相同模型自動化服務，並憑既有客戶與規模更快搶占市場。更重要的是，報稅一年只有一次，使用者平時不會持續開啟產品，也很少在報稅季結束後立刻更換服務商。這些特性讓新創難以快速建立口碑與持續成長，J.D. 因而認定這門生意很難發展成具創投規模的企業。

在有限的決策窗口承認失敗

第一個報稅季結束後，J.D. 與共同創辦人花了一週散步、喝咖啡，思考創業與人生。他們認為報稅團隊在公司裡已沒有長遠前景，於是決定轉向。J.D. 坦言，當時這感覺像是親手把事情搞砸了；但他創業的初衷，是對世界帶來正面影響、做出真正有用的產品。既然不再相信原來的方向能做到這一點，就很難繼續帶領團隊前進。

轉型也意味著必須面對團隊成員的機會成本。J.D. 最難熬的，是走進會議室看著同事，親口承認他們失敗了。不過，他後來明白，只要協助員工尋找下一份工作並提供合理資遣，坦承決策並沒有想像中可怕，反而是正確的選擇。

報稅業的季節性也迫使他們不能一再拖延。若等到四月才轉向，便已對客戶承諾要替他們報稅；若拖到隔年一月，也可能已與合作夥伴簽約。因此，他們只有約一個月的決策窗口，集中在十月十五日前後。窗口一旦關閉，就得再等一年；這種時間壓力讓他們必須在兩條可能的未來之間迅速做出選擇。

從客戶抱怨中找到新產品方向

轉型後，公司沒有更名，仍稱為 T。他們認真探索了約四個點子，最後聚焦於一個問題：為什麼還沒有人打造真正能以電子郵件和行事曆為核心的優秀產品？這個想法來自報稅客戶的日常需求：客戶雖然讚賞報稅自動化，卻仍花很多時間安排會議、回想先前談過的內容，也常重複詢問相同問題。

團隊開始思考如何用 AI 協助會前準備、會後跟進，以及回覆簡單郵件。當時模型與代理技術已能處理許多工作，他們沒有先花時間計算市場規模，而是依據大量使用者回饋，決定集中投入幾個月。隨著探索深入，他們發現銷售、商務開發與招募等面向外部的工作，往往依賴大量電子郵件與跨公司協作，因此認為這個市場不只龐大，也有全球發展的可能。

以使用者體驗打開企業市場

團隊接著思考應採取產品主導成長，還是直接銷售給企業。他們認為，付錢的人不一定是每天使用產品的人；若只討好決策者，忽略實際使用者，產品體驗便可能很糟。共同創辦人曾在 Dropbox 工作，學到的核心原則是先打造一流的消費者產品體驗，再設法滿足企業需求；反過來，若一開始只從合規與 IT 要求出發，很難做出讓使用者喜愛的產品。

因此，T 的策略是先把產品做好，並確保資料與隱私安全可靠，再讓成長自然發生。他們相信，執行長會希望公司員工也能使用自己在生活中體驗過的個人助理服務。接下來的難題，則是如何從少數企業交易擴大規模，並滿足不同公司的資料、安全與隱私要求。

AI 助理的普及與市場擴張

對話以 iPhone 問世作比喻：當年有人不相信昂貴手機會有人買，但許多執行長在生活中體驗 iPhone 的魅力後，便要求公司設法支援。AI 也可能先在個人生活中展現價值，再逐步進入職場。不過，企業導入 AI 比使用手機複雜，代理要發揮效用，必須取得資料與商業系統 API 的存取權，企業也會要求稽核紀錄、機密資訊控管與成本管理。

因此，T 先讓使用者連結電子郵件與行事曆，親自體驗產品帶來的價值，再從需求較少、採用速度較快的中小企業與中型公司切入，逐步建立產品體驗與自助成長，之後再以安全和合規能力爭取大型企業。J.D. 也指出，代理產品雖已吸引全球數百萬使用者，但整體採用仍處於早期；就像 iPhone 的普及，使用者可能需要六個月至一年半，才會真正感受到 AI 的力量。

Garry Tan 分享自己雖有行政助理，仍不太放心讓對方查看所有電子郵件；他也曾以為要去參加晚宴，卻發現活動根本沒被寫進行事曆，只因自己沒有回覆邀請郵件。這說明個人助理市場看似有限，實際需求卻可能十分普遍。J.D. 以「傑文斯悖論」說明，效率提升未必會減少需求，反而可能讓人做更多事情；他希望打造能與人自然協作的產品，讓人們發現更多適合運用 AI 的工作場景。影片最後談到 AI 像是分配運算資源的工具，讓人們自行決定如何運用，但字幕內容在此處中斷。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Today, I’m sharing a conversation that started when Ben Horowitz sent a message to Garry Tan, saying he’d discovered a tool called Tess that changed his life. Tan was stunned because he realized Tess was a product by Dennis Greys, and he distinctly remembered him working on enterprise tax filing—a pretty solid business—so why would the founder shut it down himself? Furthermore, Tan had led the investment in Pliant, and Greys was the former CEO of Pliant; he. was completely unaware of this development. Greys’ full name is J.D. In 2024, for his first startup, he chose enterprise tax filing, feeding corporate financial reports and contracts into a model to output a ready-to-submit tax return; it had great potential. Tax filing is all text with a lot of structured data, like financial statements and lease documents, which large models are good at handling; it took him a year to build the product. In the first year, their revenue reached one million dollars. By that projection, the second year should have hit 2.5 to 3 million. dollars. Before AI, this was a rather beautiful growth curve. But after AI arrived, the ceiling shifted. Incumbents could use the same models to automate filings for existing clients, grabbing market share much faster than a startup. So, he realized this business was destined to never reach venture-scale. For a founder, this is a critical situation. New entrants have the advantage of being faster and building unique products, but there’s a ticking clock on the wall; the key is whether you can build a reputation quickly before incumbents replicate your approach. Tax filing, however, has. a few unavoidable drawbacks. First, taxes can only be sold once a year; it’s not a daily active utility tool you open every day. You rarely see anyone bragging about how well they filed their taxes, and once the filing ends, it’s not the season people look to switch tax firms; by the second year , they’ve likely forgotten all about it. These gaps make massive scaling very difficult, so after the first tax season, J.D. and his co-founder spent a week walking and drinking coffee, seriously reflecting on the meaning of life, entrepreneurship, and capitalism. Ultimately, they realized one thing: the tax team had no future at this. company, so they decided to switch to a market more worth pursuing. Land says this was a remarkably brave decision that most people wouldn't make, especially since it seemed doomed at the time. His response was frank: at that moment, it felt like failure; it felt like he had truly messed up. He kept asking himself, why am I doing this? The answer was to have a positive impact on the world and build something useful to help others. Since he no longer believed they could make such an impact, that conviction faded. Then there was the team; everyone had their own opportunity costs and could have joined many other excellent companies. If the founder no longer believes in the result, walking into the meeting room every day and looking people in the eye becomes the hardest part— admitting we failed. But once you actually say it, you realize: who cares what others think of you? You can help employees find their next job and provide decent severance. After things settled, he realized this wasn't the difficult decision he initially thought ; it was the right one. Another key factor was time pressure. Taxes are collected annually, and that specific point in time was the only window they had to make a decision. They couldn't wait until April 16th to pivot after.

telling many people they would handle their taxes, nor could they wait until January after signing half their partners. So, the window was only about a month long, centered around October 15th. During that time, they lived in two universes: one continuing with taxes, and the other with no way back. Once the window passed, the door closed . He knew clearly that if the industry weren't subject to seasonal fluctuations, people would always tell themselves to wait a month, then three weeks, but they didn't have that luxury . When the window vanished, they had to decide immediately. Otherwise, they would still be in the same place a year later. In the end, they didn't change. the company name; it's still called T. So, what happened in the journey from then to the T we see today? They seriously explored about four ideas and finally settled on one question: why hasn't anyone built a great product that truly runs on email and calendars? This idea didn't come out of thin air. When they were building the tax product , many clients would say, "It's amazing that you automated taxes!" Clients still spent huge amounts of time scheduling meetings. During meetings, I often forgot what we discussed previously. Clients were always asking the same tax questions; it would be great if you could provide the answers in advance. These requirements are not. complicated to implement; it's just that at the time, no one had applied powerful AI to these common workflows, such as meeting prep, follow-ups, or replying to simple emails. They began exploring this around the time of the OPOS 4.5 release. By then, agents were already able to independently complete a lot of work on the coding side. They didn't sit down to calculate the potential market size; they just gathered a wealth of user feedback and decided to go all-in for the next few months. As they pushed forward, they found that most enterprise emails and calendars were packed, especially for. outward-facing roles like sales, business development, and recruiting, where cross-company collaboration relies mainly on email. So, they concluded the potential market size must be huge, and not just in the U.S., but worldwide. The next question was: product-led growth or direct enterprise sales? Their judgment was that the customer is the one writing the check, while the user is the one engaging with the product daily. If the customer isn't the user, you’ll likely end up with a terrible product that makes decision-makers happy but frustrates the actual users. The co-founder came from Dropbox, and the most important. lesson learned there is to always lead with a world-class consumer product experience, then figure out what it means for the enterprise. Conversely, starting from corporate compliance and IT requirements to build a product with a great user experience is almost impossible. Therefore, their focus has always been on making the product good enough; growth will naturally follow. They ensure data and privacy are secure and reliable first. They are betting on consumer expectations; CEOs look to the personal assistants they’ve used in their own lives and want the same for their companies. So the question now. becomes something else: how do you move from single enterprise deals to scale, and how do you meet the data, privacy, and security demands of other enterprises? Lear added an observation: when the iPhone launched in 2007, Steve Ballmer said no one would buy a phone that cost that much, but BlackBerry was soon finished. The explanation is that that Christmas, many CEOs received an iPhone or similar gift, took photos of their kids, were blown away, and immediately said, "I'm the boss, find a way to make these things work in the company." Others remained skeptical,.

saying AI doesn't seem that useful, and that they prefer using software like Notion instead. It feels like the iPhone has already arrived, and people are experiencing the wonders of AI in their personal lives, but that feeling hasn't reached the workplace yet. J leveraged a company called GTechnology to articulate this concern; it was an early enterprise email client for the iPhone, which he described as ridiculously ugly. He brought it up to say this isn't just about the beauty of the UI; sometimes a good product doesn't guarantee a good business, and he emphasized that the pace of change is limited by human speed. In other. words, the agent category already has millions of users worldwide, but it is still in a very early stage of adoption . Just like the iPhone, it might take six, 12, or 18 months for most people to personally feel that magic, but once they do, the question arises: how do we implement this within a company? This is more complex than the iPhone because , for an agent to be effective, it needs access to data and the APIs that power business operations. So, their approach is to talk about the journey itself first. They let users at a company link their email and calendar to experience enough value. At the. enterprise level, there are audit logs, confidential information that cannot be shared with agents, and cost controls required by the CFO; by moving down-market, the target customers shift to SMBs and mid-market companies, which have far fewer requirements and faster adoption. His current bet is to perfect the product experience, rely on self-serve growth to penetrate the lower end of the market, and then win over enterprises from a security and compliance perspective. Regarding the assistant role, Lan shared his own experience; he has an administrative assistant, but even so, he doesn't feel comfortable letting them see all his emails. When he was in London, he. thought he was going to a dinner party, but it wasn't on his calendar at all— the reason was simply that he hadn't replied to the email. So, he says the market for administrative assistants seems small because most people don't have one, but if you actually build it, the scale could be quite massive. Here, there is a Jevons paradox: when the efficiency of steam engines improved, people thought coal demand would drop, but it actually increased a thousandfold because more things could be accomplished efficiently. His definition of the market is to build a product that interacts well with people , helping them find more opportunities to apply AI in their work. In a sense, AI is like a token allocation machine,. letting people decide for themselves where to spend their tokens. As the cost of tokens drops, there will be more and more places where they can be used. He gave an example: before every meeting, you'd prepare meeting notes. An administrative assistant wouldn't do this because it's too labor-intensive, but with a large language model, the cost is very low. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OjuLyy5ajYA

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解創業者如何在產品已有營收時，仍判斷市場天花板並果斷轉型。
  • 看見人工智慧如何改變既有產業競爭，也為電子郵件與行事曆等日常工作帶來新機會。
  • 從產品策略、企業導入與使用者體驗，理解打造 AI 助理產品的關鍵取捨。

摘要

看似成功的報稅新創，為何選擇轉型

Da Fei 分享了一段由 Ben Horowitz 與 Garry Tan 的對話引出的故事：Horowitz 說一款名為 Tess 的工具改變了他的生活，Tan 才發現這是 J.D. Greys 的新產品。Greys 曾經營企業報稅新創，也曾擔任 Pliant 執行長，Tan 卻完全不知道他已轉換方向。

2024 年，J.D. 與共同創辦人打造企業報稅產品，讓客戶上傳財務報表、合約等資料，再由模型產出可提交的稅表。報稅流程高度依賴文字與結構化資料，十分適合大型模型處理；產品花了一年打造，第一年營收便達一百萬美元，照原本走勢，第二年可能達到兩百五十萬至三百萬美元。

然而，AI 也讓既有報稅業者能運用相同模型自動化服務，並憑既有客戶與規模更快搶占市場。更重要的是，報稅一年只有一次，使用者平時不會持續開啟產品，也很少在報稅季結束後立刻更換服務商。這些特性讓新創難以快速建立口碑與持續成長，J.D. 因而認定這門生意很難發展成具創投規模的企業。

在有限的決策窗口承認失敗

第一個報稅季結束後，J.D. 與共同創辦人花了一週散步、喝咖啡，思考創業與人生。他們認為報稅團隊在公司裡已沒有長遠前景，於是決定轉向。J.D. 坦言，當時這感覺像是親手把事情搞砸了；但他創業的初衷，是對世界帶來正面影響、做出真正有用的產品。既然不再相信原來的方向能做到這一點，就很難繼續帶領團隊前進。

轉型也意味著必須面對團隊成員的機會成本。J.D. 最難熬的，是走進會議室看著同事，親口承認他們失敗了。不過，他後來明白，只要協助員工尋找下一份工作並提供合理資遣，坦承決策並沒有想像中可怕，反而是正確的選擇。

報稅業的季節性也迫使他們不能一再拖延。若等到四月才轉向，便已對客戶承諾要替他們報稅；若拖到隔年一月，也可能已與合作夥伴簽約。因此，他們只有約一個月的決策窗口，集中在十月十五日前後。窗口一旦關閉，就得再等一年；這種時間壓力讓他們必須在兩條可能的未來之間迅速做出選擇。

從客戶抱怨中找到新產品方向

轉型後，公司沒有更名，仍稱為 T。他們認真探索了約四個點子，最後聚焦於一個問題：為什麼還沒有人打造真正能以電子郵件和行事曆為核心的優秀產品？這個想法來自報稅客戶的日常需求：客戶雖然讚賞報稅自動化，卻仍花很多時間安排會議、回想先前談過的內容，也常重複詢問相同問題。

團隊開始思考如何用 AI 協助會前準備、會後跟進，以及回覆簡單郵件。當時模型與代理技術已能處理許多工作，他們沒有先花時間計算市場規模，而是依據大量使用者回饋，決定集中投入幾個月。隨著探索深入，他們發現銷售、商務開發與招募等面向外部的工作，往往依賴大量電子郵件與跨公司協作，因此認為這個市場不只龐大，也有全球發展的可能。

以使用者體驗打開企業市場

團隊接著思考應採取產品主導成長，還是直接銷售給企業。他們認為，付錢的人不一定是每天使用產品的人；若只討好決策者，忽略實際使用者，產品體驗便可能很糟。共同創辦人曾在 Dropbox 工作，學到的核心原則是先打造一流的消費者產品體驗，再設法滿足企業需求；反過來，若一開始只從合規與 IT 要求出發，很難做出讓使用者喜愛的產品。

因此，T 的策略是先把產品做好，並確保資料與隱私安全可靠，再讓成長自然發生。他們相信，執行長會希望公司員工也能使用自己在生活中體驗過的個人助理服務。接下來的難題，則是如何從少數企業交易擴大規模，並滿足不同公司的資料、安全與隱私要求。

AI 助理的普及與市場擴張

對話以 iPhone 問世作比喻：當年有人不相信昂貴手機會有人買，但許多執行長在生活中體驗 iPhone 的魅力後，便要求公司設法支援。AI 也可能先在個人生活中展現價值，再逐步進入職場。不過，企業導入 AI 比使用手機複雜，代理要發揮效用，必須取得資料與商業系統 API 的存取權，企業也會要求稽核紀錄、機密資訊控管與成本管理。

因此，T 先讓使用者連結電子郵件與行事曆，親自體驗產品帶來的價值，再從需求較少、採用速度較快的中小企業與中型公司切入，逐步建立產品體驗與自助成長，之後再以安全和合規能力爭取大型企業。J.D. 也指出，代理產品雖已吸引全球數百萬使用者，但整體採用仍處於早期；就像 iPhone 的普及，使用者可能需要六個月至一年半，才會真正感受到 AI 的力量。

Garry Tan 分享自己雖有行政助理，仍不太放心讓對方查看所有電子郵件；他也曾以為要去參加晚宴，卻發現活動根本沒被寫進行事曆，只因自己沒有回覆邀請郵件。這說明個人助理市場看似有限，實際需求卻可能十分普遍。J.D. 以「傑文斯悖論」說明，效率提升未必會減少需求，反而可能讓人做更多事情；他希望打造能與人自然協作的產品，讓人們發現更多適合運用 AI 的工作場景。影片最後談到 AI 像是分配運算資源的工具，讓人們自行決定如何運用，但字幕內容在此處中斷。

So the question now. becomes something else: how do you move from single enterprise deals to scale, and how do you meet the data, privacy, and security demands of other enterprises? Lear added an observation: when the iPhone launched in 2007, Steve Ballmer said no one would buy a phone that cost that much, but BlackBerry was soon finished. The explanation is that that Christmas, many CEOs received an iPhone or similar gift, took photos of their kids, were blown away, and immediately said, "I'm the boss, find a way to make these things work in the company." Others remained skeptical,.

saying AI doesn't seem that useful, and that they prefer using software like Notion instead. It feels like the iPhone has already arrived, and people are experiencing the wonders of AI in their personal lives, but that feeling hasn't reached the workplace yet. J leveraged a company called GTechnology to articulate this concern; it was an early enterprise email client for the iPhone, which he described as ridiculously ugly. He brought it up to say this isn't just about the beauty of the UI; sometimes a good product doesn't guarantee a good business, and he emphasized that the pace of change is limited by human speed. In other. words, the agent category already has millions of users worldwide, but it is still in a very early stage of adoption . Just like the iPhone, it might take six, 12, or 18 months for most people to personally feel that magic, but once they do, the question arises: how do we implement this within a company? This is more complex than the iPhone because , for an agent to be effective, it needs access to data and the APIs that power business operations. So, their approach is to talk about the journey itself first. They let users at a company link their email and calendar to experience enough value. At the. enterprise level, there are audit logs, confidential information that cannot be shared with agents, and cost controls required by the CFO; by moving down-market, the target customers shift to SMBs and mid-market companies, which have far fewer requirements and faster adoption. His current bet is to perfect the product experience, rely on self-serve growth to penetrate the lower end of the market, and then win over enterprises from a security and compliance perspective. Regarding the assistant role, Lan shared his own experience; he has an administrative assistant, but even so, he doesn't feel comfortable letting them see all his emails. When he was in London, he. thought he was going to a dinner party, but it wasn't on his calendar at all— the reason was simply that he hadn't replied to the email. So, he says the market for administrative assistants seems small because most people don't have one, but if you actually build it, the scale could be quite massive. Here, there is a Jevons paradox: when the efficiency of steam engines improved, people thought coal demand would drop, but it actually increased a thousandfold because more things could be accomplished efficiently. His definition of the market is to build a product that interacts well with people , helping them find more opportunities to apply AI in their work. In a sense, AI is like a token allocation machine,. letting people decide for themselves where to spend their tokens. As the cost of tokens drops, there will be more and more places where they can be used. He gave an example: before every meeting, you'd prepare meeting notes. An administrative assistant wouldn't do this because it's too labor-intensive, but with a large language model, the cost is very low. So, people who need them can suddenly have notes prepared for every meeting, and they can even check who else attended. These routine tasks become valuable simply because they’ve become so much cheaper. Their job is to constantly find these opportunities and then ask the user, " Would you like us to help you with this. ?" He used the example of a restaurant owner. If you run a restaurant in the US, wholesalers send an email every month or a price list for all inventory items every quarter. There are thousands of items, and prices are always changing. Theoretically, your part-time accountant should check for price changes every quarter to see if you can order from other suppliers or if you're overpaying because something went up 20%to 30%. But in most cases, you don't do it because it's too tedious and outside your core operations. With AI, you only need to.

run an analysis once a month, and you get results in five minutes. Even if it finds nothing for 11 out of 12 months, it's still worth doing because it only costs about a dollar to run. And in that one month when it does find something, it can help you save hundreds or even thousands of dollars. When discussing products and growth, the conversation turned to horizontal versus vertical strategies. Their stance is clear: they don't want to be labeled as a company that just helps you save money on groceries. They prefer to start horizontally, learning from thousands of users and tens of thousands of businesses, then let the market decide the vertical direction. In his view, the functionality of most AI products will become increasingly similar. The unit of value has shifted from software to intelligence; as software becomes abstracted, its value drops, making it harder to lead the market with a single feature. So, how do you build a successful company? Their answer is that as AI advances, products can be better customized for each individual user. Whether you are an electrician, a venture capitalist, or an admin assistant, the tasks that can be automated are all different. This isn't done well yet; if you ask a model directly, you only get superficial advice. That’s why they don't look at individual user data, but. rather aggregate metrics, identifying active users on the platform to talk to them. Talk to ten seasoned restaurant operators, and you’ll find they all do five common things, which can be turned into an automated workflow called a restaurant owner’s daily routine. When someone joins, the system determines if you resemble a restaurant owner and then presents a polished plan before you. AI is still improving, and as the number of things it can do grows from five to fifteen. Dependency on external libraries decreases, and eventually, it will be able to deliver 80%of custom software. He compares this to the lab's FTE approach: sending. someone into your company to learn the business and use AI to develop custom software. If you pay OpenAI $ 5 million a year for FTEs, it seems cost-effective now, but as models improve, this method will become increasingly inferior. They have chosen an approach that leans more toward automation, which has much better scalability. Next is comparing why their product is better than OpenAI's or Anthropic's. Especially since they all have connectors now that can link to applications like Slack. The analogy used is the relationship between infrastructure and the application layer; Cisco and Akamai are infrastructure companies. When. companies like Amazon and eBay rose in the 90s, Cisco never thought about opening bookstores or building auction sites itself. We are in a strange era where infrastructure is turning into applications, and competing with your own suppliers is risky. A short but not-so-great answer is that the user experience surrounding email and calendars is vastly different, which others haven't truly focused on; but that's just a simple answer, as someone at OpenAI or Anthropic could wake up any day and decide to do that too. A better answer is to go back to customer needs: talk to a mid-market company. with 500 to 1,000 employees and ask them which model provider will be the best in the next three to five years. They probably won't be able to answer that. So, if you buy an OpenAI product, are you locked into using OpenAI's models forever? What if it's not the best one? That’s why they position themselves as neutral applications, using whichever provider is best for you at the time—not just for general intelligence, but also for who is stronger in voice, video, or slide capabilities, keeping the decision-making power in your hands. The second stance is that ownership belongs to you: data, memory, and context. In the past, companies owned physical assets and human resources;

now, there's a new category, perhaps called "context," which is the AI understanding everything about your business. He believes you should own this entire bucket of assets. If there is a better solution than theirs, switching over takes only a day. Those who deploy FTEs for you are actually trying to make it harder for you to switch. The third part is training; a sufficiently large company won't use you as an experiment, and if you get drawn into their gravity, it’s like selling the key to your business success to others, so "T" doesn't do training. The final position concerns competition; their view on the relationship between humans and AI might be more forward-looking than that. of the labs. Within "T," there is a product called Teams, which is built around an internal customer relationship management system. They trust agents to decide what information a company possesses, or whether other employees can use it; for example, if you ask in "T,""Does anyone know someone on the finance team?" Who is this potential client? "T" assistants can see other employees 'agents and help you find people relevant to your lead. Although this feature is powerful , from a privacy perspective, the design must be exceptional. Their idea is to let people operate at the speed of AI; in the past, if you asked in Slack or Teams, "Does anyone know. someone on that team?" You would have to wait about a day for a response, whereas with "T," you get an immediate reply because they decided to rely on AI to handle security and internal company privacy for these types of questions. "T" sees the future as having far less human intervention than today, and their job is to get companies to embrace that world, as the economic benefits far outweigh the risks. For most large companies, it makes no sense to truly rely on any single lab. There is a "Goldilocks" zone of relevance here. Assume your revenue is $ 1 trillion, then you are. certainly the number one target for labs, but if your revenue is zero and nobody uses your product, they won't care at all. Coding has already crossed that line, and Anthropic is investing heavily in it, clearly impossible to ignore; but healthcare, law, and coding are all massive fields, and labs are almost forced to make these big bets, leading to horizontal fragmentation, making it hard to dig deep into small markets. Finally, the two discussed a more subtle issue: distribution is never uniform. Lan says many people talk about crossing the chasm, but this isn't the kind of technology that exists in one place and not others; people all over the world are using it, just unevenly distributed. JD gave an example of a vacation rental company where someone uses "T" to compare photos of surfboards or beach buggies for damage to decide whether to refund a deposit. This was not on his wish list at all. What unlocked this demand was someone in that small business who just loved to tinker. He was struck by this, then discussed with his assistant how to automate image comparison. We see such use cases in all sorts of strange corners of the economy; the problem lies here: the world lacks enough tinkerers, people with the time to fuss over their own businesses, and. that is why AI hasn't reached mass adoption. Even though Claude or ChatGPT have been around for 12 months and many small businesses could use them to save more time, they just treat them as a better Google search. The reason is that the product experience cannot just be a text box. You can't teach others; you can only demonstrate the value proposition and do the work for them. So why keep users in the loop? They link emails and calendars, ideally connecting to a business operating system, to build a custom integration that isn't out-of-the-box but works like magic. This is the reason for the.

uneven distribution. In Silicon Valley, everyone works with engineers and is closer to that natural hands-on capability, but most of the world lacks this condition. If you can enable someone who doesn't like to tinker to access AI and get the same value as a tinkerer, you could potentially build a massive company. Because AI can solve many business problems, intelligence itself is ready-made; the key lies in how to deploy it effectively at scale. Lampert mentioned a very brilliant professor he met at Harvard who, when asked about AI, said he tried it years ago and it was okay but not great. Then. , Lampert had him use AI to rewrite a paper he wrote over 20 years ago; he said it was fantastic, but upon learning it was ChatGPT, he couldn't believe it. AI progress is too fast; many people are used to judging it by current standards, whereas Silicon Valley tends to judge where it will be in the future. There is another large group that only sees it as it is now, and ironically, part of the reason is that early adopters tried it once two years ago, saw hallucinations and errors, and remained stuck in that version of reality. If they tried it again now, the results would be completely different. The judgment here. is that ultimate victory lies in continuous development, keeping the business equipped with the best current AI, and our perceptions of what is possible, hard, or easy will be completely overturned. He gave the example of Airbnb. In the past two and a half months, intelligent assistants can do things that were almost impossible six months ago, with success rates climbing from about 30%to 90%. So , for the demo, he's picking things out for you, and you're surprised—don't you need a user interface? But these things are hard to sell; you have to be very specific, like saying, "I can use your paid Canva subscription to make. those posters you always create with CW , do you want me to do that?" Five minutes later, and for just 25 cents, it produces something quite valuable. Things that seem increasingly impossible are actually just following the trend of what current models can do for you. Lair then steered the conversation toward agent traffic. He said that, in a broad sense, agent traffic has already far exceeded human traffic. He used Yahoo Finance as an example: Yahoo pays Nasdaq to get stock quotes and provides them to you for free, on the condition that you give them your attention and view their ads. However, this contract has already been broken. Both sides of the contract are in opposition, but there are opportunities for synergy hidden within . This is like a brand new search engine optimization; if you can become a recipient of agent traffic instead of blocking it, and instead figure out how to welcome it, that is a huge opportunity. Following this logic, Amazon's loss should be Walmart's gain, because Walmart has no ad business and different incentives; the most interesting part here is, what happens if the agent's information is not neutral? For example, if you have an MTA agent, and the MTA has tons of ads. —United Airlines advertises on the MTA more than any other airline—and you ask it to book a flight, what happens once you realize the information it gives you is no longer neutral? Human motives will always exist; there will always be someone who wants to sell and market things. So he believes what you need is a neutral, personal agent of your own. With no other sources of funding, your wallet is its only funding source, so it will have the incentive to give you the best information without being distorted by sales forces. Then he touched on adversarial versus non-adversarial, putting it into the framework of experience. Some friction is enjoyable,.

like browsing between shops while out, while other friction is what people don't want to spend time on, like ordering toilet paper at home where you just want to get the items into your cart as quickly as possible. It is not always about pursuing maximum efficiency. If he were Amazon, facing an advertising business of around $ 70 billion a year, he would say we shouldn't block AI agents, but blocking them creates even more pressure, so we need to create a different experience where you can actually see ads within them. However, the development of AI is simply too fast; it will change distribution methods and human habits at a speed no one can predict, and. there will surely be some who fail miserably. He finds another category interesting, which is M, a free personal AI agent. People might wonder, will Meta eventually run ads on M? But perhaps it's not needed at all; maybe M just provides data to help them target you better on Instagram. Users don't open Instagram for efficiency, but for fun, and so monetization and the intelligent experience are separated in this way. And platforms like Amazon are at a disadvantage, at least on the AI agent side. If you are just a supply aggregator, this may no longer be a. good business model. Their real response should be to own their own private AI agent. To give an example, there is a website called CamelCamelCamel that tracks Amazon prices, with 20 million users in the US alone. You tell it, "I want to know if Dr. Pepper is $ 8 right now; let me know when it drops to $ 6." It won't place the order for you; it will just send you a notification. Some people have more time than money, while others have more money than time. People with more money and less time won't use CamelCamelCamel; only those with more time will. If you now let the AI agents of every busy, wealthy person handle. these tools for them, they will certainly use them; it’s practically an IQ test. The common takeaway from all this is that the value of supply aggregation has greatly diminished, because human attention is limited, and now it can be replaced by automation. Having talked this far, this episode is coming to a close. Looking at the entire conversation, the path is actually quite clear: a good business that held up in the old world may not necessarily grow into a venture-scale company once AI compresses the window of advantage. So, he chose to proactively shut it down, completed the pivot in one month, and turned the. customer's internal complaints into profit. I’ve laid out a few industry assessments: clients and users must be distinguished, model access should be neutral, data memory and context ownership must remain with the user, and the traffic generated by AI agents is rewriting the old advertising contracts driven by eyeballs. Whether these judgments hold true will take time to verify, but there is a question worth leaving for everyone: when the interests of your AI agent and the platform's agent conflict, what will you choose? Will you continue using. that free assistant, which can be distorted by marketing, or are you willing to pay a little for an impartial intelligence? Welcome.
