https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OjuLyy5ajYA

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解創業者如何在產品已有營收時，仍判斷市場天花板並果斷轉型。
  • 看見人工智慧如何改變既有產業競爭，也為電子郵件與行事曆等日常工作帶來新機會。
  • 從產品策略、企業導入與使用者體驗，理解打造 AI 助理產品的關鍵取捨。

摘要

看似成功的報稅新創，為何選擇轉型

Da Fei 分享了一段由 Ben Horowitz 與 Garry Tan 的對話引出的故事：Horowitz 說一款名為 Tess 的工具改變了他的生活，Tan 才發現這是 J.D. Greys 的新產品。Greys 曾經營企業報稅新創，也曾擔任 Pliant 執行長，Tan 卻完全不知道他已轉換方向。

2024 年，J.D. 與共同創辦人打造企業報稅產品，讓客戶上傳財務報表、合約等資料，再由模型產出可提交的稅表。報稅流程高度依賴文字與結構化資料，十分適合大型模型處理；產品花了一年打造，第一年營收便達一百萬美元，照原本走勢，第二年可能達到兩百五十萬至三百萬美元。

然而，AI 也讓既有報稅業者能運用相同模型自動化服務，並憑既有客戶與規模更快搶占市場。更重要的是，報稅一年只有一次，使用者平時不會持續開啟產品，也很少在報稅季結束後立刻更換服務商。這些特性讓新創難以快速建立口碑與持續成長，J.D. 因而認定這門生意很難發展成具創投規模的企業。

在有限的決策窗口承認失敗

第一個報稅季結束後，J.D. 與共同創辦人花了一週散步、喝咖啡，思考創業與人生。他們認為報稅團隊在公司裡已沒有長遠前景，於是決定轉向。J.D. 坦言，當時這感覺像是親手把事情搞砸了；但他創業的初衷，是對世界帶來正面影響、做出真正有用的產品。既然不再相信原來的方向能做到這一點，就很難繼續帶領團隊前進。

轉型也意味著必須面對團隊成員的機會成本。J.D. 最難熬的，是走進會議室看著同事，親口承認他們失敗了。不過，他後來明白，只要協助員工尋找下一份工作並提供合理資遣，坦承決策並沒有想像中可怕，反而是正確的選擇。

報稅業的季節性也迫使他們不能一再拖延。若等到四月才轉向，便已對客戶承諾要替他們報稅；若拖到隔年一月，也可能已與合作夥伴簽約。因此，他們只有約一個月的決策窗口，集中在十月十五日前後。窗口一旦關閉，就得再等一年；這種時間壓力讓他們必須在兩條可能的未來之間迅速做出選擇。

從客戶抱怨中找到新產品方向

轉型後，公司沒有更名，仍稱為 T。他們認真探索了約四個點子，最後聚焦於一個問題：為什麼還沒有人打造真正能以電子郵件和行事曆為核心的優秀產品？這個想法來自報稅客戶的日常需求：客戶雖然讚賞報稅自動化，卻仍花很多時間安排會議、回想先前談過的內容，也常重複詢問相同問題。

團隊開始思考如何用 AI 協助會前準備、會後跟進，以及回覆簡單郵件。當時模型與代理技術已能處理許多工作，他們沒有先花時間計算市場規模，而是依據大量使用者回饋，決定集中投入幾個月。隨著探索深入，他們發現銷售、商務開發與招募等面向外部的工作，往往依賴大量電子郵件與跨公司協作，因此認為這個市場不只龐大，也有全球發展的可能。

以使用者體驗打開企業市場

團隊接著思考應採取產品主導成長，還是直接銷售給企業。他們認為，付錢的人不一定是每天使用產品的人；若只討好決策者，忽略實際使用者，產品體驗便可能很糟。共同創辦人曾在 Dropbox 工作，學到的核心原則是先打造一流的消費者產品體驗，再設法滿足企業需求；反過來，若一開始只從合規與 IT 要求出發，很難做出讓使用者喜愛的產品。

因此，T 的策略是先把產品做好，並確保資料與隱私安全可靠，再讓成長自然發生。他們相信，執行長會希望公司員工也能使用自己在生活中體驗過的個人助理服務。接下來的難題，則是如何從少數企業交易擴大規模，並滿足不同公司的資料、安全與隱私要求。

AI 助理的普及與市場擴張

對話以 iPhone 問世作比喻：當年有人不相信昂貴手機會有人買，但許多執行長在生活中體驗 iPhone 的魅力後，便要求公司設法支援。AI 也可能先在個人生活中展現價值，再逐步進入職場。不過，企業導入 AI 比使用手機複雜，代理要發揮效用，必須取得資料與商業系統 API 的存取權，企業也會要求稽核紀錄、機密資訊控管與成本管理。

因此，T 先讓使用者連結電子郵件與行事曆，親自體驗產品帶來的價值，再從需求較少、採用速度較快的中小企業與中型公司切入，逐步建立產品體驗與自助成長，之後再以安全和合規能力爭取大型企業。J.D. 也指出，代理產品雖已吸引全球數百萬使用者，但整體採用仍處於早期；就像 iPhone 的普及，使用者可能需要六個月至一年半，才會真正感受到 AI 的力量。

Garry Tan 分享自己雖有行政助理，仍不太放心讓對方查看所有電子郵件；他也曾以為要去參加晚宴，卻發現活動根本沒被寫進行事曆，只因自己沒有回覆邀請郵件。這說明個人助理市場看似有限，實際需求卻可能十分普遍。J.D. 以「傑文斯悖論」說明，效率提升未必會減少需求，反而可能讓人做更多事情；他希望打造能與人自然協作的產品，讓人們發現更多適合運用 AI 的工作場景。影片最後談到 AI 像是分配運算資源的工具，讓人們自行決定如何運用，但字幕內容在此處中斷。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Partners, I’m Da Fei. Today, I’m sharing a conversation that started when Ben Horowitz sent a message to Garry Tan, saying he’d discovered a tool called Tess that changed his life. Tan was stunned because he realized Tess was a product by Dennis Greys, and he distinctly remembered him working on enterprise tax filing—a pretty solid business—so why would the founder shut it down himself? Furthermore, Tan had led the investment in Pliant, and Greys was the former CEO of Pliant; he. was completely unaware of this development. Greys’ full name is J.D. In 2024, for his first startup, he chose enterprise tax filing, feeding corporate financial reports and contracts into a model to output a ready-to-submit tax return; it had great potential. Tax filing is all text with a lot of structured data, like financial statements and lease documents, which large models are good at handling; it took him a year to build the product. In the first year, their revenue reached one million dollars. By that projection, the second year should have hit 2.5 to 3 million. dollars. Before AI, this was a rather beautiful growth curve. But after AI arrived, the ceiling shifted. Incumbents could use the same models to automate filings for existing clients, grabbing market share much faster than a startup. So, he realized this business was destined to never reach venture-scale. For a founder, this is a critical situation. New entrants have the advantage of being faster and building unique products, but there’s a ticking clock on the wall; the key is whether you can build a reputation quickly before incumbents replicate your approach. Tax filing, however, has. a few unavoidable drawbacks. First, taxes can only be sold once a year; it’s not a daily active utility tool you open every day. You rarely see anyone bragging about how well they filed their taxes, and once the filing ends, it’s not the season people look to switch tax firms; by the second year , they’ve likely forgotten all about it. These gaps make massive scaling very difficult, so after the first tax season, J.D. and his co-founder spent a week walking and drinking coffee, seriously reflecting on the meaning of life, entrepreneurship, and capitalism. Ultimately, they realized one thing: the tax team had no future at this. company, so they decided to switch to a market more worth pursuing. Land says this was a remarkably brave decision that most people wouldn't make, especially since it seemed doomed at the time. His response was frank: at that moment, it felt like failure; it felt like he had truly messed up. He kept asking himself, why am I doing this? The answer was to have a positive impact on the world and build something useful to help others. Since he no longer believed they could make such an impact, that conviction faded. Then there was the team; everyone had their own opportunity costs and could have joined many other excellent companies. If the founder no longer believes in the result, walking into the meeting room every day and looking people in the eye becomes the hardest part— admitting we failed. But once you actually say it, you realize: who cares what others think of you? You can help employees find their next job and provide decent severance. After things settled, he realized this wasn't the difficult decision he initially thought ; it was the right one. Another key factor was time pressure. Taxes are collected annually, and that specific point in time was the only window they had to make a decision. They couldn't wait until April 16th to pivot after.

telling many people they would handle their taxes, nor could they wait until January after signing half their partners. So, the window was only about a month long, centered around October 15th. During that time, they lived in two universes: one continuing with taxes, and the other with no way back. Once the window passed, the door closed . He knew clearly that if the industry weren't subject to seasonal fluctuations, people would always tell themselves to wait a month, then three weeks, but they didn't have that luxury . When the window vanished, they had to decide immediately. Otherwise, they would still be in the same place a year later. In the end, they didn't change. the company name; it's still called T. So, what happened in the journey from then to the T we see today? They seriously explored about four ideas and finally settled on one question: why hasn't anyone built a great product that truly runs on email and calendars? This idea didn't come out of thin air. When they were building the tax product , many clients would say, "It's amazing that you automated taxes!" Clients still spent huge amounts of time scheduling meetings. During meetings, I often forgot what we discussed previously. Clients were always asking the same tax questions; it would be great if you could provide the answers in advance. These requirements are not. complicated to implement; it's just that at the time, no one had applied powerful AI to these common workflows, such as meeting prep, follow-ups, or replying to simple emails. They began exploring this around the time of the OPOS 4.5 release. By then, agents were already able to independently complete a lot of work on the coding side. They didn't sit down to calculate the potential market size; they just gathered a wealth of user feedback and decided to go all-in for the next few months. As they pushed forward, they found that most enterprise emails and calendars were packed, especially for. outward-facing roles like sales, business development, and recruiting, where cross-company collaboration relies mainly on email. So, they concluded the potential market size must be huge, and not just in the U.S., but worldwide. The next question was: product-led growth or direct enterprise sales? Their judgment was that the customer is the one writing the check, while the user is the one engaging with the product daily. If the customer isn't the user, you’ll likely end up with a terrible product that makes decision-makers happy but frustrates the actual users. The co-founder came from Dropbox, and the most important. lesson learned there is to always lead with a world-class consumer product experience, then figure out what it means for the enterprise. Conversely, starting from corporate compliance and IT requirements to build a product with a great user experience is almost impossible. Therefore, their focus has always been on making the product good enough; growth will naturally follow. They ensure data and privacy are secure and reliable first. They are betting on consumer expectations; CEOs look to the personal assistants they’ve used in their own lives and want the same for their companies. So the question now. becomes something else: how do you move from single enterprise deals to scale, and how do you meet the data, privacy, and security demands of other enterprises? Lear added an observation: when the iPhone launched in 2007, Steve Ballmer said no one would buy a phone that cost that much, but BlackBerry was soon finished. The explanation is that that Christmas, many CEOs received an iPhone or similar gift, took photos of their kids, were blown away, and immediately said, "I'm the boss, find a way to make these things work in the company." Others remained skeptical,.

saying AI doesn't seem that useful, and that they prefer using software like Notion instead. It feels like the iPhone has already arrived, and people are experiencing the wonders of AI in their personal lives, but that feeling hasn't reached the workplace yet. J leveraged a company called GTechnology to articulate this concern; it was an early enterprise email client for the iPhone, which he described as ridiculously ugly. He brought it up to say this isn't just about the beauty of the UI; sometimes a good product doesn't guarantee a good business, and he emphasized that the pace of change is limited by human speed. In other. words, the agent category already has millions of users worldwide, but it is still in a very early stage of adoption . Just like the iPhone, it might take six, 12, or 18 months for most people to personally feel that magic, but once they do, the question arises: how do we implement this within a company? This is more complex than the iPhone because , for an agent to be effective, it needs access to data and the APIs that power business operations. So, their approach is to talk about the journey itself first. They let users at a company link their email and calendar to experience enough value. At the. enterprise level, there are audit logs, confidential information that cannot be shared with agents, and cost controls required by the CFO; by moving down-market, the target customers shift to SMBs and mid-market companies, which have far fewer requirements and faster adoption. His current bet is to perfect the product experience, rely on self-serve growth to penetrate the lower end of the market, and then win over enterprises from a security and compliance perspective. Regarding the assistant role, Lan shared his own experience; he has an administrative assistant, but even so, he doesn't feel comfortable letting them see all his emails. When he was in London, he. thought he was going to a dinner party, but it wasn't on his calendar at all— the reason was simply that he hadn't replied to the email. So, he says the market for administrative assistants seems small because most people don't have one, but if you actually build it, the scale could be quite massive. Here, there is a Jevons paradox: when the efficiency of steam engines improved, people thought coal demand would drop, but it actually increased a thousandfold because more things could be accomplished efficiently. His definition of the market is to build a product that interacts well with people , helping them find more opportunities to apply AI in their work. In a sense, AI is like a token allocation machine,. letting people decide for themselves where to spend their tokens. As the cost of tokens drops, there will be more and more places where they can be used. He gave an example: before every meeting, you'd prepare meeting notes. An administrative assistant wouldn't do this because it's too labor-intensive, but with a large language model, the cost is very low. So, people who need them can suddenly have notes prepared for every meeting, and they can even check who else attended. These routine tasks become valuable simply because they’ve become so much cheaper. Their job is to constantly find these opportunities and then ask the user, " Would you like us to help you with this. ?" He used the example of a restaurant owner. If you run a restaurant in the US, wholesalers send an email every month or a price list for all inventory items every quarter. There are thousands of items, and prices are always changing. Theoretically, your part-time accountant should check for price changes every quarter to see if you can order from other suppliers or if you're overpaying because something went up 20%to 30%. But in most cases, you don't do it because it's too tedious and outside your core operations. With AI, you only need to.

run an analysis once a month, and you get results in five minutes. Even if it finds nothing for 11 out of 12 months, it's still worth doing because it only costs about a dollar to run. And in that one month when it does find something, it can help you save hundreds or even thousands of dollars. When discussing products and growth, the conversation turned to horizontal versus vertical strategies. Their stance is clear: they don't want to be labeled as a company that just helps you save money on groceries. They prefer to start horizontally, learning from thousands of users and tens of thousands of businesses, then let the market decide the vertical direction. In his view, the functionality of most AI products will become increasingly similar. The unit of value has shifted from software to intelligence; as software becomes abstracted, its value drops, making it harder to lead the market with a single feature. So, how do you build a successful company? Their answer is that as AI advances, products can be better customized for each individual user. Whether you are an electrician, a venture capitalist, or an admin assistant, the tasks that can be automated are all different. This isn't done well yet; if you ask a model directly, you only get superficial advice. That’s why they don't look at individual user data, but. rather aggregate metrics, identifying active users on the platform to talk to them. Talk to ten seasoned restaurant operators, and you’ll find they all do five common things, which can be turned into an automated workflow called a restaurant owner’s daily routine. When someone joins, the system determines if you resemble a restaurant owner and then presents a polished plan before you. AI is still improving, and as the number of things it can do grows from five to fifteen. Dependency on external libraries decreases, and eventually, it will be able to deliver 80%of custom software. He compares this to the lab's FTE approach: sending. someone into your company to learn the business and use AI to develop custom software. If you pay OpenAI $ 5 million a year for FTEs, it seems cost-effective now, but as models improve, this method will become increasingly inferior. They have chosen an approach that leans more toward automation, which has much better scalability. Next is comparing why their product is better than OpenAI's or Anthropic's. Especially since they all have connectors now that can link to applications like Slack. The analogy used is the relationship between infrastructure and the application layer; Cisco and Akamai are infrastructure companies. When. companies like Amazon and eBay rose in the 90s, Cisco never thought about opening bookstores or building auction sites itself. We are in a strange era where infrastructure is turning into applications, and competing with your own suppliers is risky. A short but not-so-great answer is that the user experience surrounding email and calendars is vastly different, which others haven't truly focused on; but that's just a simple answer, as someone at OpenAI or Anthropic could wake up any day and decide to do that too. A better answer is to go back to customer needs: talk to a mid-market company. with 500 to 1,000 employees and ask them which model provider will be the best in the next three to five years. They probably won't be able to answer that. So, if you buy an OpenAI product, are you locked into using OpenAI's models forever? What if it's not the best one? That’s why they position themselves as neutral applications, using whichever provider is best for you at the time—not just for general intelligence, but also for who is stronger in voice, video, or slide capabilities, keeping the decision-making power in your hands. The second stance is that ownership belongs to you: data, memory, and context. In the past, companies owned physical assets and human resources;

now, there's a new category, perhaps called "context," which is the AI understanding everything about your business. He believes you should own this entire bucket of assets. If there is a better solution than theirs, switching over takes only a day. Those who deploy FTEs for you are actually trying to make it harder for you to switch. The third part is training; a sufficiently large company won't use you as an experiment, and if you get drawn into their gravity, it’s like selling the key to your business success to others, so "T" doesn't do training. The final position concerns competition; their view on the relationship between humans and AI might be more forward-looking than that. of the labs. Within "T," there is a product called Teams, which is built around an internal customer relationship management system. They trust agents to decide what information a company possesses, or whether other employees can use it; for example, if you ask in "T,""Does anyone know someone on the finance team?" Who is this potential client? "T" assistants can see other employees 'agents and help you find people relevant to your lead. Although this feature is powerful , from a privacy perspective, the design must be exceptional. Their idea is to let people operate at the speed of AI; in the past, if you asked in Slack or Teams, "Does anyone know. someone on that team?" You would have to wait about a day for a response, whereas with "T," you get an immediate reply because they decided to rely on AI to handle security and internal company privacy for these types of questions. "T" sees the future as having far less human intervention than today, and their job is to get companies to embrace that world, as the economic benefits far outweigh the risks. For most large companies, it makes no sense to truly rely on any single lab. There is a "Goldilocks" zone of relevance here. Assume your revenue is $ 1 trillion, then you are. certainly the number one target for labs, but if your revenue is zero and nobody uses your product, they won't care at all. Coding has already crossed that line, and Anthropic is investing heavily in it, clearly impossible to ignore; but healthcare, law, and coding are all massive fields, and labs are almost forced to make these big bets, leading to horizontal fragmentation, making it hard to dig deep into small markets. Finally, the two discussed a more subtle issue: distribution is never uniform. Lan says many people talk about crossing the chasm, but this isn't the kind of technology that exists in one place and not others; people all over the world are using it, just unevenly distributed. JD gave an example of a vacation rental company where someone uses "T" to compare photos of surfboards or beach buggies for damage to decide whether to refund a deposit. This was not on his wish list at all. What unlocked this demand was someone in that small business who just loved to tinker. He was struck by this, then discussed with his assistant how to automate image comparison. We see such use cases in all sorts of strange corners of the economy; the problem lies here: the world lacks enough tinkerers, people with the time to fuss over their own businesses, and. that is why AI hasn't reached mass adoption. Even though Claude or ChatGPT have been around for 12 months and many small businesses could use them to save more time, they just treat them as a better Google search. The reason is that the product experience cannot just be a text box. You can't teach others; you can only demonstrate the value proposition and do the work for them. So why keep users in the loop? They link emails and calendars, ideally connecting to a business operating system, to build a custom integration that isn't out-of-the-box but works like magic. This is the reason for the.

uneven distribution. In Silicon Valley, everyone works with engineers and is closer to that natural hands-on capability, but most of the world lacks this condition. If you can enable someone who doesn't like to tinker to access AI and get the same value as a tinkerer, you could potentially build a massive company. Because AI can solve many business problems, intelligence itself is ready-made; the key lies in how to deploy it effectively at scale. Lampert mentioned a very brilliant professor he met at Harvard who, when asked about AI, said he tried it years ago and it was okay but not great. Then. , Lampert had him use AI to rewrite a paper he wrote over 20 years ago; he said it was fantastic, but upon learning it was ChatGPT, he couldn't believe it. AI progress is too fast; many people are used to judging it by current standards, whereas Silicon Valley tends to judge where it will be in the future. There is another large group that only sees it as it is now, and ironically, part of the reason is that early adopters tried it once two years ago, saw hallucinations and errors, and remained stuck in that version of reality. If they tried it again now, the results would be completely different. The judgment here. is that ultimate victory lies in continuous development, keeping the business equipped with the best current AI, and our perceptions of what is possible, hard, or easy will be completely overturned. He gave the example of Airbnb. In the past two and a half months, intelligent assistants can do things that were almost impossible six months ago, with success rates climbing from about 30%to 90%. So , for the demo, he's picking things out for you, and you're surprised—don't you need a user interface? But these things are hard to sell; you have to be very specific, like saying, "I can use your paid Canva subscription to make. those posters you always create with CW , do you want me to do that?" Five minutes later, and for just 25 cents, it produces something quite valuable. Things that seem increasingly impossible are actually just following the trend of what current models can do for you. Lair then steered the conversation toward agent traffic. He said that, in a broad sense, agent traffic has already far exceeded human traffic. He used Yahoo Finance as an example: Yahoo pays Nasdaq to get stock quotes and provides them to you for free, on the condition that you give them your attention and view their ads. However, this contract has already been broken. Both sides of the contract are in opposition, but there are opportunities for synergy hidden within . This is like a brand new search engine optimization; if you can become a recipient of agent traffic instead of blocking it, and instead figure out how to welcome it, that is a huge opportunity. Following this logic, Amazon's loss should be Walmart's gain, because Walmart has no ad business and different incentives; the most interesting part here is, what happens if the agent's information is not neutral? For example, if you have an MTA agent, and the MTA has tons of ads. —United Airlines advertises on the MTA more than any other airline—and you ask it to book a flight, what happens once you realize the information it gives you is no longer neutral? Human motives will always exist; there will always be someone who wants to sell and market things. So he believes what you need is a neutral, personal agent of your own. With no other sources of funding, your wallet is its only funding source, so it will have the incentive to give you the best information without being distorted by sales forces. Then he touched on adversarial versus non-adversarial, putting it into the framework of experience. Some friction is enjoyable,.

like browsing between shops while out, while other friction is what people don't want to spend time on, like ordering toilet paper at home where you just want to get the items into your cart as quickly as possible. It is not always about pursuing maximum efficiency. If he were Amazon, facing an advertising business of around $ 70 billion a year, he would say we shouldn't block AI agents, but blocking them creates even more pressure, so we need to create a different experience where you can actually see ads within them. However, the development of AI is simply too fast; it will change distribution methods and human habits at a speed no one can predict, and. there will surely be some who fail miserably. He finds another category interesting, which is M, a free personal AI agent. People might wonder, will Meta eventually run ads on M? But perhaps it's not needed at all; maybe M just provides data to help them target you better on Instagram. Users don't open Instagram for efficiency, but for fun, and so monetization and the intelligent experience are separated in this way. And platforms like Amazon are at a disadvantage, at least on the AI agent side. If you are just a supply aggregator, this may no longer be a. good business model. Their real response should be to own their own private AI agent. To give an example, there is a website called CamelCamelCamel that tracks Amazon prices, with 20 million users in the US alone. You tell it, "I want to know if Dr. Pepper is $ 8 right now; let me know when it drops to $ 6." It won't place the order for you; it will just send you a notification. Some people have more time than money, while others have more money than time. People with more money and less time won't use CamelCamelCamel; only those with more time will. If you now let the AI agents of every busy, wealthy person handle. these tools for them, they will certainly use them; it’s practically an IQ test. The common takeaway from all this is that the value of supply aggregation has greatly diminished, because human attention is limited, and now it can be replaced by automation. Having talked this far, this episode is coming to a close. Looking at the entire conversation, the path is actually quite clear: a good business that held up in the old world may not necessarily grow into a venture-scale company once AI compresses the window of advantage. So, he chose to proactively shut it down, completed the pivot in one month, and turned the. customer's internal complaints into profit. I’ve laid out a few industry assessments: clients and users must be distinguished, model access should be neutral, data memory and context ownership must remain with the user, and the traffic generated by AI agents is rewriting the old advertising contracts driven by eyeballs. Whether these judgments hold true will take time to verify, but there is a question worth leaving for everyone: when the interests of your AI agent and the platform's agent conflict, what will you choose? Will you continue using. that free assistant, which can be distorted by marketing, or are you willing to pay a little for an impartial intelligence? Welcome.

摘要

新模型登場，額度爭議搶走焦點

作者以 Kimi K3.1 Pro 發布後引發的「額度已用完」討論開場。部分付費用戶表示，199 元甚至 699 元的會員方案，額度仍可能在短時間內耗盡，讓使用體驗與價格是否相稱受到質疑。另一方面，海外宣傳也因疑似要求創作者隱瞞付費合作而引發批評。

能力提升與定價取捨

作者介紹，K3.1 Pro 延續 K3 的 MoE 架構，透過大量後訓練與強化學習提升能力；模型總參數約 2.8 萬億，每次推理啟用約 1040 億參數。它在 Terminal-Bench 4.0 等測試中表現突出，也展現長程程式設計、3D 建模及物理模擬等能力。不過，部分科學基準仍落後於頂尖海外模型，官方公布的測試成績也未必能完全代表每位用戶的實際體驗。

產品同步推出速度更快、價格也更高的版本，思考模式則無法完全關閉；官方並承諾開源模型權重。API 價格雖較前代下降，仍高於 DeepSeek、MiniMax 等國內競品。由於模型可能產生較長的思考內容，單次任務的實際成本未必隨標價下降，會員額度與 API 費用因此成為使用者關注的焦點。

高成本能力與商業化壓力

作者指出，月之暗面正嘗試以高成本維持高能力，再以較高定價支撐商業化，並將海外市場視為重要戰場。隨著海外收入占比提高、年化經常性收入（ARR）突破 10 億美元，公司仍須在模型能力、收入成長與有限算力之間取捨。這也使付費用戶的額度體驗，成為商業策略能否成立的重要考驗。

算力短缺從何而來

算力不足並非新問題。作者回顧，月之暗面在 2024 年走紅時，便曾因資源有限而無法承接部分企業合作。如今模型邁向萬億級參數，程式設計等智慧體又會讀取大量檔案、反覆除錯並調用多個子代理，單次任務可能消耗數百萬個 Token，使算力需求進一步攀升。

隨著大模型由聊天工具轉為持續工作的生產力工具，Token 消耗量顯著增加，使用成本也不再只是看單價，而要看完成整項任務所需的計算資源。面對美國科技巨頭較充足的基礎設施，中國企業則更需要透過 MoE、MLA 等架構與工程優化，以及開源生態，盡可能提升算力使用效率。

國產算力與使用建議

作者提到，華為昇騰 950 系列、平頭哥真武 V900 等國產晶片正在追趕，但先進製程、光刻設備與封裝等環節仍限制整體供應能力。即使智慧體可協助優化推理設施，產業仍面臨算力供給成長追不上消耗速度的競賽。

作者最後總結，Kimi K3.1 Pro 在後訓練與程式設計任務上展現進步，但額度爭議、定價策略與算力限制仍是其商業化挑戰。由於官方數據多來自特定測試，使用者若要導入工作流程，宜先以小規模任務實測效果與成本，再決定是否擴大使用。

產品同步推出速度更快、價格也更高的版本，思考模式則無法完全關閉；官方並承諾開源模型權重。API 價格雖較前代下降，仍高於 DeepSeek、MiniMax 等國內競品。由於模型可能產生較長的思考內容，單次任務的實際成本未必隨標價下降，會員額度與 API 費用因此成為使用者關注的焦點。

高成本能力與商業化壓力

作者指出，月之暗面正嘗試以高成本維持高能力，再以較高定價支撐商業化，並將海外市場視為重要戰場。隨著海外收入占比提高、年化經常性收入（ARR）突破 10 億美元，公司仍須在模型能力、收入成長與有限算力之間取捨。這也使付費用戶的額度體驗，成為商業策略能否成立的重要考驗。

算力短缺從何而來

算力不足並非新問題。作者回顧，月之暗面在 2024 年走紅時，便曾因資源有限而無法承接部分企業合作。如今模型邁向萬億級參數，程式設計等智慧體又會讀取大量檔案、反覆除錯並調用多個子代理，單次任務可能消耗數百萬個 Token，使算力需求進一步攀升。

隨著大模型由聊天工具轉為持續工作的生產力工具，Token 消耗量顯著增加，使用成本也不再只是看單價，而要看完成整項任務所需的計算資源。面對美國科技巨頭較充足的基礎設施，中國企業則更需要透過 MoE、MLA 等架構與工程優化，以及開源生態，盡可能提升算力使用效率。

國產算力與使用建議

作者提到，華為昇騰 950 系列、平頭哥真武 V900 等國產晶片正在追趕，但先進製程、光刻設備與封裝等環節仍限制整體供應能力。即使智慧體可協助優化推理設施，產業仍面臨算力供給成長追不上消耗速度的競賽。

作者最後總結，Kimi K3.1 Pro 在後訓練與程式設計任務上展現進步，但額度爭議、定價策略與算力限制仍是其商業化挑戰。由於官方數據多來自特定測試，使用者若要導入工作流程，宜先以小規模任務實測效果與成本，再決定是否擴大使用。
